title: Hash, encryption, signature
summary: Three tools that look alike and answer different questions: is it unchanged, who can read it, who wrote it.

text: A hash is a fingerprint of data: always the same for the same bytes, completely different if one bit changes.
- It can't be turned back into the data, and it isn't secret: anyone can compute it.
- Uses: check a download is unchanged (against a hash from a place you trust), store passwords (the system keeps a slow, salted hash of yours: guessing takes years, not seconds), name git commits.

scheme: both sides need the same secret:
how do you get it to the other one?
text: Encryption hides the content: only someone with the key can read it back.
- With one shared secret (symmetric encryption), it's fast: disks, archives, a file locked with a passphrase.
- The hard part is passing the secret: by mail, anyone who reads the mail can read the file.

scheme: ├── public key     give it to anyone
└── private key    only you have it
text: Key pairs solve that: two halves made together, a public one to give away and a private one to keep.
- What Sam's public key locks, only Sam's private key opens. No secret had to travel.
- You can't compute the private key from the public one.
- HTTPS uses both: key pairs to agree on a fresh secret, then fast symmetric encryption.

scheme: signature   which key signed it, unchanged?
text: A signature works the other way round: only the private key signs, anyone with the public key checks.
- It proves which key signed and that nothing changed; it hides nothing. Check the key's fingerprint against a trusted source.
- apt checks the signed package list and each package's hash, dnf each package's signature. A package downloaded by hand gets no such check.
- base64 only rewrites bytes as plain letters: anyone decodes it. It protects nothing.
